overview: This lab placed ESXi, a Type 1 hypervisor, inside a Workstation VM and then created a nested Windows Server VM inside ESXi. The most useful part of the exercise was separating management-network failures from storage and guest power-on failures.
environment: Windows host → VMware Workstation → nested ESXi
VMFS datastore and Windows Server guest

steps.title: Prepare the outer ESXi VM
steps.description: I created the VMware VM for ESXi and configured its storage and NAT networking. The retained baseline capture shows 4 GB memory, four processors and a 40 GB disk.

steps.title: Enable nested virtualization and install ESXi
steps.description: My setup notes describe exposing hardware virtualization to the ESXi guest, attaching its installer, selecting the installation disk and completing the hypervisor installation. No root password is published.

steps.title: Identify the management endpoint
steps.description: I used the ESXi direct console to identify its private management address after startup.

steps.title: Restore host-to-ESXi network access
steps.description: When the Host Client was unreachable, I checked the typed address, host IP configuration and the VMnet8 host adapter. My troubleshooting notes record restoring that adapter and the VMware networking services.

steps.title: Open the ESXi Host Client
steps.description: After restoring management reachability, I accessed the local HTTPS Host Client and inspected the host’s configuration and available storage.

steps.title: Prepare usable datastore capacity
steps.description: I investigated the missing/free-space datastore problem and provisioned separate storage for the VMFS datastore rather than relying on the small ESXi system disk.

steps.title: Upload the guest installation image
steps.description: I used the datastore browser to upload Windows Server installation media for the nested guest.

steps.title: Create and configure the Windows guest
steps.description: I used Create / Register VM and configured the guest resources. The captured settings show two vCPUs, 4096 MB memory and a 27 GB disk at that stage.

steps.title: Investigate the failed power-on
steps.description: I inspected the detailed MonitorLoop task error. The recorded No space left on device message identified insufficient space for the guest’s swap file, beyond the already allocated media and virtual disk.

steps.title: Resolve the recorded resource constraints
steps.description: The notes describe recreating the guest on a larger datastore and resolving host virtualization-feature conflicts. The datastore change addressed the explicit swap-allocation failure.

steps.title: Power on the nested guest
steps.description: The final retained capture shows the Windows Server guest powered on at the Windows boot logo inside the ESXi console.

steps.title: Record the limits of the final capture
steps.description: I used the console and Host Client resource views to check guest startup. The report describes Windows setup, but the supplied image does not show its completed installation or a final desktop.

checks.title: ESXi management access
checks.description: The direct console and Host Client captures show the running hypervisor and its reachable management interface.

checks.title: Guest configuration and power-on
checks.description: The screenshots show the guest resource settings and Windows boot logo.

checks.title: Networking and datastore remediation
checks.description: The written notes describe restoring VMnet8 connectivity and resolving the datastore/swap allocation errors.

lessons: Nested virtualization has distinct outer-host, hypervisor and inner-guest resource dependencies.
A browser timeout can originate in virtual networking rather than the management service.
Datastore planning must include installation media, guest disks and swap-file space.
Detailed task errors provide stronger diagnostic evidence than a generic power-on failure label.
scope: The report’s planned 8 GB/eight-processor and 40 GB guest profiles differ from the retained captures. I present the pictured settings as stage-specific observations, not final recommended allocations. The 27 GB guest disk is below the published 32 GB Windows Server baseline. The final image proves boot activity, not a completed OS installation or a performance benchmark.

troubleshooting.title: The ESXi management page timed out
troubleshooting.symptom: The typed address contained an incorrect octet, and connectivity still failed after the typo was corrected. The host’s VMnet8 adapter was missing from the recorded IP configuration.
troubleshooting.action: I corrected the URL, restored the VMnet8 host virtual adapter in Virtual Network Editor and restarted the VMware DHCP and NAT services.
troubleshooting.result: My notes record ping replies and successful Host Client access after the virtual network was restored.

troubleshooting.title: No usable datastore space was available
troubleshooting.symptom: The initial disk left no suitable free area for a guest datastore. A small later datastore could not accommodate the installation ISO and guest allocation.
troubleshooting.action: I provisioned separate, larger virtual storage and created a VMFS datastore with headroom for the guest and its media.
troubleshooting.result: The report records that the installation media could be uploaded and the guest registered on the larger datastore.

troubleshooting.title: Guest power-on failed with a swap-file error
troubleshooting.symptom: The power-on task included MonitorLoop failure and an explicit inability to extend the guest swap file because the datastore had no free space.
troubleshooting.action: I addressed the datastore capacity and the host virtualization conflicts described in my troubleshooting record, then registered and powered on the guest again.
troubleshooting.result: The final supplied capture shows the nested Windows guest at its boot logo.
